check/vote: Self-consistency's vote needs each sample to be right more often than not. A model right one time in ten gives it little to work with.
check/easy: But some answers are easy to check, even when hard to find. Solving three x plus seven equals thirty one takes steps. Checking an answer takes one: plug it back in.
check/draw: So sample four answers: six, eight, nine and seven.
check/check: Plug each one in. Three times eight, plus seven, is thirty one, so eight passes. The other three miss.
check/name: A checker like this is called a verifier. Draw some number of samples, n, and keep one the verifier accepts: that is best-of-n.
check/tests: Code can be checked too: run each program against its tests.
check/chen: In 2021, Mark Chen and colleagues at OpenAI scored a code model this way. With one sample per problem, it solved twenty eight point eight percent. Counting a problem solved when any of a hundred samples passed, it solved seventy point two percent.
odds/p: How often does best-of-n find a right answer? Say each sample is right with chance p, here zero point three, independently of the others.
odds/wrong: With a perfect verifier, best-of-n fails only when every sample is wrong. One sample is wrong with chance one minus p: zero point seven.
odds/miss: Independent chances multiply, so all four are wrong with zero point seven to the fourth: about zero point two four.
odds/hit: That is the only way it fails, so it succeeds with one minus that: zero point seven six, from a model right less than a third of the time.
odds/formula: With n samples in place of four, a hit has chance one minus, one minus p, to the n.
odds/add: Chances do not simply add: four times zero point three is one point two, more than certain. Samples can be right together, and one is all it takes.
many/curve: Draw more, and the chance climbs, but each sample adds less than the one before: it can only cut what is left of the miss.
many/target: To be right ninety percent of the time, the miss must fall to a tenth or less. Find the smallest n that gets it there.
many/six: zero point seven to the sixth is about zero point one two: still above a tenth, so six samples give only zero point eight eight.
many/seven: zero point seven to the seventh is about zero point zero eight, so seven samples are right ninety two percent of the time: the smallest n.
many/rare: It works even where a vote cannot: at p of zero point one, twenty samples include a right answer eighty eight percent of the time.
trust/fooled: All this assumed a verifier that is never wrong. Say instead it is fooled by one wrong answer in five.
trust/pool: Count a hundred samples at p of zero point three. Thirty are right, and all of them pass. Seventy are wrong, and one in five of those gets through: fourteen.
trust/share: So of the forty four that pass, thirty are right: thirty over forty four, about zero point six eight.
trust/level: More samples add both kinds in that same mix, so the answer kept stays right about zero point six eight of the time, however large n gets.
trust/cobbe: In 2021, Karl Cobbe and colleagues at OpenAI trained a second model as the verifier for grade-school math word problems.
trust/limit: Past about four hundred samples per problem, more samples stopped paying off: the search began to find wrong answers that fooled it.
trust/strict: A verifier that rejects some right answers does far less harm. Nothing wrong is kept, so success still climbs toward one, as if right answers were rarer.
trust/must: So above all, a verifier must reject the wrong ones.
